title: When to name a pattern
summary: Name a pattern only after you can state the design problem it solves.

parts.rule: A design pattern names a recurring design problem and a proven arrangement of responsibilities. Explain the changing requirement first, then the pattern's mechanics, then its cost. The name is useful shorthand only after the listener understands why a plain function, conditional, or constructor is no longer enough.
parts.why: Pattern recognition helps people discuss a design quickly, but pattern-first answers often add classes without improving changeability. Interviewers are evaluating judgment: can you connect a likely change to a structure, compare a simpler option, and acknowledge new indirection? The goal is a design that fits, not the largest number of named patterns.
parts.example: Case 1: Checkout supports flat-rate, weight-based, and courier-distance shipping, and a fourth policy is planned. The workflow stays fixed while one calculation varies. Name Strategy, show ShippingStrategy.quote(), and mention the cost of one abstraction plus selection logic. Case 2: a page has one isCompact flag that chooses 8 px or 16 px spacing. A conditional or spacing function is enough; two strategy classes would make the rule harder to find. Case 3: a text editor must undo the last 50 actions and replay them after a crash. Name Command because each edit needs to be stored with execute or reversal data; also budget memory for history and define what happens when an external action cannot be undone. A strong spoken answer is: “Shipping formulas change independently, so I would inject a strategy. That keeps Checkout stable, at the cost of another interface. If we only had one boolean rule, I would keep the conditional.” This sequence demonstrates the requirement, structure, tradeoff, and simpler alternative. The same test works for other patterns: Adapter needs an interface mismatch, Observer needs a changing set of listeners, and Builder needs genuinely complex construction.
parts.use: Use a pattern name when it clarifies a recurring relationship, several variants already exist or are credible, and the structure makes testing or change safer. Draw the participating roles and walk one call or state transition. Mention the simpler design you considered so the choice is grounded in the current problem.
parts.refuse: Do not introduce a pattern solely because a familiar word appears in the requirements. Avoid wrapping one stable function in several interfaces, predicting hypothetical variants with no evidence, or using a name as a substitute for explaining data flow. If you cannot state the change pressure and the added cost, keep the design concrete and simple.

body:
Rule. A design pattern names a recurring design problem and a proven arrangement of responsibilities. Explain the changing requirement first, then the pattern's mechanics, then its cost. The name is useful shorthand only after the listener understands why a plain function, conditional, or constructor is no longer enough.

Why it matters. Pattern recognition helps people discuss a design quickly, but pattern-first answers often add classes without improving changeability. Interviewers are evaluating judgment: can you connect a likely change to a structure, compare a simpler option, and acknowledge new indirection? The goal is a design that fits, not the largest number of named patterns.

Worked example. Case 1: Checkout supports flat-rate, weight-based, and courier-distance shipping, and a fourth policy is planned. The workflow stays fixed while one calculation varies. Name Strategy, show ShippingStrategy.quote(), and mention the cost of one abstraction plus selection logic. Case 2: a page has one isCompact flag that chooses 8 px or 16 px spacing. A conditional or spacing function is enough; two strategy classes would make the rule harder to find. Case 3: a text editor must undo the last 50 actions and replay them after a crash. Name Command because each edit needs to be stored with execute or reversal data; also budget memory for history and define what happens when an external action cannot be undone. A strong spoken answer is: “Shipping formulas change independently, so I would inject a strategy. That keeps Checkout stable, at the cost of another interface. If we only had one boolean rule, I would keep the conditional.” This sequence demonstrates the requirement, structure, tradeoff, and simpler alternative. The same test works for other patterns: Adapter needs an interface mismatch, Observer needs a changing set of listeners, and Builder needs genuinely complex construction.

[[diagram:force]]

When to use. Use a pattern name when it clarifies a recurring relationship, several variants already exist or are credible, and the structure makes testing or change safer. Draw the participating roles and walk one call or state transition. Mention the simpler design you considered so the choice is grounded in the current problem.

When to refuse. Do not introduce a pattern solely because a familiar word appears in the requirements. Avoid wrapping one stable function in several interfaces, predicting hypothetical variants with no evidence, or using a name as a substitute for explaining data flow. If you cannot state the change pressure and the added cost, keep the design concrete and simple.
